chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyah (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar said: He narrated to me Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Al-Hussein ibn Yazid al-Nawfaly, from Isma'il ibn Muslim al-Sakoony, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his forefathers, from Ali (peace be upon them).

He said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) was asked, 'Which wealth is best?' He said: 'Crops that their owner cultivates and improves, and pays its due on the day of harvest.' It was said: 'Then which wealth is best after crops?' He said: 'A man with his flock of sheep, who follows them to grazing lands, establishes prayer, and pays alms-tax.' It was said: 'Then which wealth is best after sheep?' He said: 'Cows that go forth with good and return with good.' It was said: 'Then which wealth is best after cows?' He said: 'Palm trees deeply rooted in the soil and well-fed in their place; excellent are the palm trees. Whoever sells them, their price is like dust on the head of a mountain, which the wind scatters on a stormy day, unless he replaces them.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, then which wealth is best after palm trees?' He remained silent. A man said to him: 'What about camels?' He said: 'In them is misery, roughness, and exertion, and distance from the dwelling. They go forth retreating and return retreating. Their good comes only from their left side. Indeed, they do not lack the wretched sinners.'
ai.seo_question: What are the four best forms of wealth according to the Prophet in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Khisal*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) establishes a hierarchy of wealth based on agricultural productivity and ease of management, culminating in a nuanced evaluation of camels. While camels are acknowledged as valuable assets, they are characterized by 'shiqā' (hardship/misery) and 'jafā' (roughness), reflecting the Shia scholarly view that their high maintenance and mobility make them less spiritually and practically optimal than stationary, cultivated wealth like crops and palm trees.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 4-105 Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyih - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Ibrahim ibn Hashim, on the authority of Al-Hussein ibn Yazid al-Nawfaly, on the authority of Isma’il ibn Muslim al-Sakoony,on the authority of Ja’far ibn Muhammad (MGB) , on the authority of his father (MGB) , on the authority of his forefathers (MGB), on the authority of Ali (MGB),

“God’s Prophet (MGB) was asked, ‘What is the best form of wealth?’ The Prophet (MGB) replied, ‘What one cultivates for himself and has paid its alms-tax when he picks it.’ The Prophet (MGB) was asked, ‘What is the next best form of wealth?’ He (MGB) replied, ‘Flocks of sheep which one herds himself in pastures where he prays, and for which he pays the alms-tax.’ He (MGB) was asked, ‘What is the best form of wealth after sheep?’ The Prophet (MGB) replied, ‘Cows which give milk in the morning and at night.’ He (MGB) was asked, ‘O Prophet of God! What is the best form of wealth after cows?’ The Prophet (MGB) replied, ‘Tall palm trees which are deeply rooted in the ground. Whoever sells these trees, what he gets in return is as the dust on top of the mountain which would scatter around with the slightest wind: unless he buys another palm field instead.’ He (MGB) was asked, ‘O Prophet of God! What is the best form of wealth after date palms?’ The Prophet (MGB) remained silent. A man asked, ‘How about camels?’ The Prophet (MGB) said, ‘Owning camels involves a lot of misery, hardship, and exertion. You must take it far away in the morning and night. It lives in the desert. It has no use except for its unfortunate owners to worry that it may be harmed.’”
